overview: This file documents the intensifying American debate in 1940 over whether and how to restrict exports that supported Japan’s war in China. It combines State, Commerce, and Navy Department correspondence; trade statistics; corporate shipment reports; internal legal and policy memoranda; congressional inquiries; and a large body of petitions, organizational records, and publicity from embargo advocates. Particular attention falls on petroleum and aviation gasoline, scrap iron, nonferrous metals, aircraft equipment and technology, rubber, and other strategic materials; the voluntary “moral embargo”; the absence of clear statutory authority for a comprehensive embargo; possible evasions through intermediaries and overseas suppliers; and Japan’s efforts to secure alternative resources from places such as the Dutch East Indies.
keywords: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
interest: The file is especially useful because it places grassroots activism, congressional pressure, corporate conduct, and internal policymaking in the same documentary frame. The petitions and organizational lists reveal the breadth of religious, women’s, labor, peace, and China-aid mobilization, while the memoranda expose officials’ practical and legal difficulties in turning moral condemnation into enforceable policy. Corporate reports, detailed trade tables, and investigations of intermediaries also allow historians to trace the material supply networks behind Japan’s war and the emerging shift from voluntary restraint toward statutory export control.
